readAloud.text: The Silk Road was never a single road but a network of caravan routes linking China with the Mediterranean. Merchants carried silk, spices, and glass across deserts and mountain passes, and with the goods travelled ideas, religions, and technologies. The exchange of paper-making, for instance, reshaped Europe centuries later. The route declined only when sea transport became faster and cheaper.

More than thirty thousand years ago, artists painted herds of animals on the walls of caves in southern France and northern Spain. The painters worked by the light of stone lamps burning animal fat, and they ground minerals into pigments of red, black, and ochre. Remarkably, the images show careful observation of animal movement, suggesting that early humans combined artistic skill with detailed knowledge of the natural world.

Engineers classify bridges into a few basic types according to how they carry load. Beam bridges rest on piers, arch bridges transfer weight outward into the foundations, and suspension bridges hang the roadway from cables anchored at both ends. Choosing among them depends on the width of the gap, the ground beneath, and the budget available. Modern designs increasingly combine several principles in a single structure.

Sign languages are fully developed languages, not simply gestures or improvised mime. Each has its own grammar, vocabulary, and regional dialects, and they evolve independently of the spoken languages around them. Linguists have shown that children acquiring a sign language from birth reach the same developmental milestones as hearing children. This finding confirms that the human capacity for language does not depend on speech alone.

For centuries, salt was so valuable that it was sometimes called white gold. Before refrigeration, salting was the most reliable method of preserving fish and meat, which made the mineral essential to trading economies. Governments frequently taxed it, and in some countries the refusal to pay such taxes sparked protest and even rebellion. Today salt is cheap, but its historical importance survives in language and legend.

Penguins are flightless birds superbly adapted to life at sea. Their wings have become stiff, flat flippers that propel them through the water with surprising speed, while dense, waterproof feathers and a thick layer of fat insulate them against the cold. On land, however, the same bodies that make them agile swimmers leave them awkward walkers, vulnerable to predators and, in some regions, to changing ocean conditions.

The modern Olympic Games were revived in 1896 by a French educator who believed international sport could promote peace. The first competition in Athens attracted fewer than three hundred athletes, all of them men, from thirteen countries. Since then the Games have grown into the largest sporting event on Earth, and women have taken part since 1900. Each host city now invests heavily in stadiums and transport.

retellLecture.title: The history of chocolate
retellLecture.sample: The lecture traced the history of chocolate from ancient Mesoamerica, where the Maya and Aztec drank it as a bitter spiced beverage, to its arrival in Europe with Spanish explorers, where sugar made it a luxury. Solid chocolate appeared only in the nineteenth century once cocoa butter could be pressed out, and milk chocolate from Switzerland soon made it affordable for everyone.
retellLecture.text: Chocolate began as a bitter drink in ancient Mesoamerica, where the Maya and Aztec ground cacao seeds and mixed them with water and spices. Spanish explorers carried the beans to Europe in the sixteenth century, where sugar transformed the drink into a luxury for the wealthy. Solid eating chocolate did not appear until the nineteenth century, once machines could press out cocoa butter and mix the remaining solids smoothly. The invention of milk chocolate in Switzerland soon followed, and prices fell enough for ordinary families to enjoy it. Today chocolate is one of the most popular treats in the world.

retellLecture.title: The science of laughter
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained that laughter occurs when the brain detects something unexpected but harmless, which researchers call a benign violation. The speaker stressed that laughter is mostly social — people laugh far more in company than alone — and that it releases endorphins, reducing pain and stress. Even babies laugh before they can speak, showing the behaviour is deeply rooted in human development.
retellLecture.text: Laughter is far more complex than it appears. Physiologically, it is a rhythmic series of exhalations produced when the brain detects something unexpected yet harmless, a combination researchers call benign violation. Laughter is overwhelmingly social: people are about thirty times more likely to laugh in company than alone, because laughter signals trust and bonds groups together. It also triggers the release of endorphins, natural chemicals that reduce pain and produce mild pleasure, which may explain why shared laughter lowers stress and strengthens relationships. Even infants laugh long before they can speak, suggesting the behaviour is deeply rooted in human development.

respondToSituation.prompt: You are flying home for your sister's wedding tomorrow. Your connecting flight has just been cancelled, and you are standing at the airline's service desk. Speak to the agent. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: You are flying home for your sister's wedding tomorrow. Your connecting flight has just been cancelled, and you are standing at the airline's service desk. Speak to the agent. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Hi, excuse me, I hope you can help me. My connecting flight this evening has just been cancelled, and I'm supposed to be at my sister's wedding tomorrow morning. I booked the whole journey as one ticket, so I'm hoping you can rebook me. Could you check whether there's a seat on a later flight tonight, or on the first flight tomorrow morning if tonight is impossible? I only have carry-on luggage, so changing flights should be quick. If nothing works tonight, could you tell me what accommodation or compensation the airline can offer? I'd really appreciate your help — this wedding means a lot to my family.

respondToSituation.sample: Good evening. I'm afraid there's a problem with my booking. I reserved a double room for three nights — the confirmation number is in this email — but you're telling me it was cancelled. I've been travelling for more than twelve hours and it's almost midnight, so I really need somewhere to sleep tonight. Could you please speak to your manager and check whether any room has become available, even a smaller one? If the hotel is genuinely full, then as your confirmation email guarantees, I'd expect you to arrange and pay for a comparable room nearby. Could you also make sure the rest of my stay is protected? Thank you for your help.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should restaurants replace tipping with higher fixed prices and wages? Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students debated whether tipping should be abolished in favour of higher fixed wages and menu prices. Speaker A argued that tipping is unfair because income depends on customers' generosity and bias, while kitchen staff receive nothing. Speaker B defended tipping as an incentive and warned that higher listed prices would put customers off. Speaker C noted that fixed service charges already work in Europe and insisted that reform must include a liveable base wage and fair sharing across the whole team. They agreed only that staff need guaranteed pay first.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'd get rid of tipping altogether. Waiting staff should earn a proper wage from their employer, not depend on the generosity of strangers. In countries where nobody tips, service is still excellent. Tipping also lets customers treat staff unequally — studies show clear biases in who gets tipped more.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: But tipping works as an incentive. A waiter who does a brilliant job earns more than a lazy one, and customers like having that control. If you fold tips into the menu price, every restaurant looks more expensive, and people react to the headline price before anything else.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Plenty of restaurants in Europe already add a fixed service charge, and customers accept it without complaining. My bigger worry is the other side of the kitchen: in many places tips are shared with cooks and dishwashers, who are often paid even less than servers. If we reform tipping, the whole pay structure has to change.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly — back-of-house staff never see tips in most systems. A no-tipping model would let the owner distribute pay fairly across the entire team instead of leaving it to luck.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I still think many customers would object to higher menu prices, even if the total bill stayed the same. Maybe the compromise is publishing both: a service-inclusive price, plus a note that any extra tipping is purely optional.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Whatever we choose, staff need a guaranteed base wage first. Reform only works if the fixed pay is genuinely liveable, not just slightly higher than before.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: The space agency's budget must be reduced. Should priority go to robotic missions or to human spaceflight? Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The speakers discussed how the space agency should cut its budget. Speaker A favoured robotic missions, which cost a fraction of crewed flights and deliver more science per dollar. Speaker B argued that human explorers work faster than rovers and that the astronaut programme inspires future scientists, warning that cancelling it would be expensive to restart. Speaker C prioritised Earth observation satellites, which save lives and money every year. They agreed that Earth observation should be protected, while A preferred robots overall and B wanted some human programme to survive.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'd cut human spaceflight completely. A robotic probe costs a fraction of a crewed mission, needs no food, oxygen, or return ticket, and can operate for years. Every dollar spent on keeping people alive up there is a dollar not spent on science.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Robots are impressive, but they're slow. A geologist with a hammer could do in one afternoon what a rover manages in a month. And human exploration inspires generations of engineers and scientists — that's hard to put a price on.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: You're both arguing about the Moon and Mars, but the most valuable space spending is much closer to home. Weather satellites, disaster monitoring, and climate observation save lives and money every single year. That's where any reduced budget should go first.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I accept that Earth observation should be protected. But between the remaining options, unmanned missions still deliver far more knowledge per billion spent.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Fine — keep the robots running, but don't cancel the astronaut programme entirely. If we stop training crews now, the expertise disappears for decades, and restarting it later would cost far more than maintaining it.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: The bicycle, often taken for granted today, was the product of nearly a century of experimentation. Early models of the eighteen-sixties had wooden wheels mounted directly on iron frames, earning them the nickname 'boneshakers' because every bump on the road was felt by the rider. The addition of pneumatic tyres by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888 transformed comfort and speed, while the chain drive allowed wheels of equal and manageable size, ending the dangerous era of the enormous front-wheel penny-farthing. Cheap, clean, and independent of horses, the bicycle offered ordinary people unprecedented personal mobility, and historians credit it with widening both the social circle and the employment range of the working and middle classes.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Although early bicycles were uncomfortable machines whose riders felt every bump, innovations such as pneumatic tyres and the chain drive made cycling safe and pleasant, and the resulting cheap personal mobility widened the social and employment opportunities of ordinary working and middle-class people.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Antarctica is the only continent with no permanent population and no single owner, and for much of the twentieth century several nations laid overlapping claims to slices of it. During the International Geophysical Year of 1957–58, however, scientists from twelve countries cooperated so successfully that they decided to preserve that spirit. The resulting Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and in force from 1961, suspends all territorial claims, guarantees freedom of scientific investigation, and prohibits military activity and nuclear explosions on the continent. Dozens of nations have since joined, and later agreements added strict environmental protections, including a ban on mining. Many observers regard the treaty as one of the most successful examples of international cooperation in history.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Because competing territorial claims threatened Antarctica, twelve cooperating nations signed a treaty that suspends ownership disputes, guarantees free scientific research and bans military and mining activity, an agreement that later members and environmental protocols have preserved and that many consider a model of international cooperation.

essay.prompt: Some countries make voting compulsory, and citizens who do not vote may receive a small fine. Other countries leave the decision entirely to individuals. Should voting be compulsory? Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200–300 words.
essay.sample: Possible structure: (1) Introduction — paraphrase the debate, state your position. (2) Arguments for compulsory voting: turnout reflects the whole population, elections better represent everyone, campaigns focus on policies rather than chasing voters, disadvantaged groups are not outvoted by the most motivated. (3) Arguments against: voting is a personal choice, not a duty; a forced vote may be uninformed or resentful; punishing non-voters seems undemocratic; abstention can itself be a meaningful message. (4) Conclusion — your view, e.g. compulsory voting is justified because governments decide matters for everyone. Useful phrases: 'It is often argued that…', 'A further benefit is…', 'Critics respond that…', 'On balance, I believe…'

mcMultiple.passage: A map is a model of the world, and like any model it involves compromise. Because the Earth is curved but paper is flat, every projection distorts something: area, distance, direction, or shape. The famous Mercator projection, designed for navigation, keeps compass bearings straight but makes Greenland appear larger than South America, although the opposite is true. Other projections preserve accurate areas at the cost of distorted shapes. Modern cartographers often switch projections depending on purpose, and digital maps can even change projection as users zoom between continental and street level. The lesson is that no map is perfectly faithful; each one answers a particular question.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The origins of tea
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture traced the history of tea from ancient China, where it was first drunk as a medicine, through its spread to Japan by Buddhist monks and to Europe by traders in the seventeenth century. Because imports became expensive, cultivation was established in India and Ceylon, and tea is now among the most widely consumed drinks in the world.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Tea began as a medicinal drink in ancient China, where legend credits the emperor Shen Nong with its discovery when leaves drifted into his boiling water. By the Tang dynasty, tea drinking was a daily habit across China, and Buddhist monks carried the plant to Japan, where the elaborate tea ceremony developed. European traders introduced tea in the seventeenth century, and it became enormously fashionable in Britain. When imports grew expensive, cultivation spread to India and Ceylon under British control, creating the vast plantations that dominate production today. Today, tea is second only to water among the world's beverages.

summarizeSpokenText.title: Invasive cane toads
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture explained that cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 to control sugarcane beetles, but the plan failed because the toads could not reach the pests. Free from natural predators and protected by toxic skin, the toads spread widely across northern Australia, killing the predators that try to eat them, and they continue to expand despite control programmes.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Cane toads are one of the most notorious examples of a failed biological control. Native to South and Central America, they were introduced to Queensland, Australia, in 1935 to eat beetles that were damaging sugarcane crops. The plan failed almost immediately: the toads could not reach the beetles, which live high on the stalks, but the toads themselves thrived in the absence of natural predators. Their skin contains powerful toxins, so predators such as quolls and crocodiles die after eating them. The toads have since spread across vast areas of northern Australia and continue to expand their range, despite decades of control efforts.
